vignette:
Mr. A is a 53-year-old painter, South Asian, married with two grown children. He came to therapy at his wife’s urging, though he doesn’t quite see the point. “I’m not crazy,” he said in our first session, his voice flat. “I just can’t sleep.” He is a thin man, stooped, with paint-stained fingers that tremble slightly when he reaches for the cup of water I offer.

The event that fractured his life happened twenty-three years ago, during the civil war in his home country. He was a civilian, living in a northern town with his wife and young son. One afternoon, while he was painting a mural in a school courtyard—a commission from the local community—the shelling began. He remembers the sound first: a low whistle that became a screech, then a crack so loud it felt like the sky was tearing. He threw himself flat against the wall, hands over his head. When the dust settled, the courtyard was destroyed. Two children, students he had seen playing that morning, were dead. A third, a boy of eight, lay nearby with his leg crushed under rubble. Mr. A crawled to him, tried to stop the bleeding with his own shirt, but the boy died in his arms. He remembers the child’s face, the surprise in his eyes, the warmth of blood soaking through his clothes.

After that day, Mr. A never finished the mural. He left the town with his family, eventually emigrating to the United States. He took up painting again here, but it is different. In his studio—a converted garage cluttered with half-stretched canvases—he works mostly at night, when the world is quiet. He used to paint landscapes, village scenes, portraits of neighbors. Now he paints only abstract shapes in heavy, dark colors—deep browns and reds, slashes of black. He cannot bring himself to paint people. The last time he tried, a portrait of his younger daughter, he had to scrape the canvas clean halfway through. “Her face kept changing,” he told me. “It wasn’t her.”

He is a skilled painter, his hands steady on the brush, yet he cannot finish a single piece. He starts, stops, abandons. His wife tells me he used to sell his work at local galleries; now the canvases gather dust. He avoids the neighborhood art supply store because the smell of turpentine reminds him of something he cannot name. He avoids loud noises—a car backfiring on the street sends him diving for cover, heart pounding, vision gray. He has stopped going to the mosque because the closed space and the murmur of voices make him feel trapped. Crowds are impossible. The last time he attended his son’s wedding, he spent the entire reception in the bathroom, hands trembling, counting breaths.

At night, he wakes three or four times. The nightmare is always the same: the whistle, the crack, the boy’s eyes. Sometimes he wakes up on the floor, having rolled off the bed mid-dream. His wife has learned not to touch him when he thrashes. She says he moans in his sleep, words in his native language she cannot understand. He feels perpetually on guard, as if something terrible is about to happen. While painting, he cannot focus—his mind drifts to that afternoon, to the sound, to the weight of the child in his arms. He feels guilty, always, for escaping, for building a new life while those children did not. He rarely laughs anymore. His daughter says he looks through her rather than at her.

He thinks about the event every day, sometimes for hours. The image of the boy’s face surfaces without warning—while he stirs his tea, while he washes his brushes, while he lies in bed waiting for sleep. He tries to push it away, but it only returns sharper. He has stopped telling his wife. “She has heard enough,” he says. “It does not change anything.”

In our sessions, he sits with his arms crossed, often silent for long stretches. He does not like to talk about the war. He prefers to describe the texture of paint, the way light changes on a wet brush. But when I ask what he sees when he closes his eyes, he hesitates, then whispers: “The boy. The red. Always the red.”
